reference.source: Postgraduate Haematology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: An inherited red-cell membrane disorder, usually autosomal dominant, caused by defects in the horizontal cytoskeletal proteins that stabilise the membrane skeleton
The blood film shows numerous elliptical (cigar-shaped) red cells, and the diagnosis is often made incidentally on a routine film
Most heterozygotes are asymptomatic with little or no haemolysis, so anaemia is frequently absent

A subset has clinically significant chronic haemolysis, and the severe homozygous or compound-heterozygous variant hereditary pyropoikilocytosis presents in infancy with marked haemolysis and bizarre red-cell fragmentation
Underlying defects most often involve alpha- or beta-spectrin (SPTA1, SPTB) or protein 4.1 (EPB41), which weaken the horizontal linkages of the membrane skeleton
Neonates may transiently have more severe haemolysis and hyperbilirubinaemia than they will later in life
Most patients need no treatment; folate support and, in severe transfusion-dependent haemolysis, splenectomy may be considered
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary elliptocytosis results from mutations that weaken the horizontal (lateral) protein interactions of the red-cell membrane skeleton, chiefly defects in spectrin self-association (alpha- and beta-spectrin) or in protein 4.1 that impair the spectrin-actin-4.1 junctional complex. The membrane skeleton loses its ability to recover normal shape after the mechanical deformation of circulation, so cells become progressively and permanently elliptical. In more severe forms the destabilised membrane fragments under shear stress, producing poikilocytosis and shortened red-cell survival, with the spleen removing damaged cells and driving the degree of haemolytic anaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Iron deficiency anaemia (which can produce elliptocytes)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and reticulocyte count
Blood film to quantify elliptocytes and identify poikilocytosis
Markers of haemolysis including bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis
Membrane protein or spectrin studies where the phenotype is severe
Genetic testing of SPTA1, SPTB and EPB41 in selected cases
redFlags: Severe neonatal haemolysis with hyperbilirubinaemia risking kernicterus
Aplastic crisis, typically with parvovirus B19 infection, causing an abrupt fall in haemoglobin
Symptomatic anaemia with haemodynamic compromise in severe variants
Features of pyropoikilocytosis in infancy requiring urgent haematology input
reference.prognosis: The great majority of people with hereditary elliptocytosis have a normal life expectancy and require no treatment, while the minority with significant haemolysis or the pyropoikilocytosis variant may need folate, transfusion or splenectomy.
pitfalls: Dismissing elliptocytes as artefact without correlating with family history and haemolysis markers
Overlooking transient severe haemolysis in the neonatal period
Attributing anaemia entirely to the membrane disorder and missing a superimposed cause such as iron deficiency or an aplastic crisis
Recommending splenectomy in asymptomatic disease where it is not warranted
management: No treatment is needed for the asymptomatic majority with mild or absent haemolysis; provide reassurance and periodic observation
Folic acid supplementation to support erythropoiesis in those with chronic haemolysis
Red-cell transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, particularly in severe hereditary pyropoikilocytosis or marked neonatal haemolysis
Phototherapy or exchange transfusion for neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia
Splenectomy for severe transfusion-dependent haemolysis, preceded by appropriate vaccination and followed by antibiotic prophylaxis and thromboprophylaxis considerations
Monitor full blood count and reticulocytes and screen for pigment gallstones, with cholecystectomy where symptomatic
Genetic counselling for the inherited membrane defect involving SPTA1, SPTB or EPB41
